draft:
Public court records are public infrastructure rather than luxury goods. If the courthouse door is open but the digital door demands an expensive subscription, access isn't public. It's a tollbooth planted on a road we've already paid to build. You may possess the right to inspect the record, but your right is ornamental if exercising it costs more than you can spare (the person with the least money gets the thinnest version of justice).

What happens when you need to read a complaint, follow a docket, or check the order that governs your case? You encounter a market built around scarcity (fees, search charges, subscriptions). The vendor isn't selling legal insight alone; it's selling passage through a gate that should never have been private. If you can't pay, you're pushed toward summaries, fragments, or somebody else's account of what the court actually did. The record remains public while practical access belongs to customers.

Court administrators can offer the strongest defense: digitizing records costs money, search systems require maintenance, and somebody has to cover the bill. Sure, those costs are real. But charging at the point of access makes research a meter that runs fastest when your need is greatest. I can accept public spending for usable systems without accepting a model that rations scrutiny by income. Taxes, filing fees, and legislative appropriations are public financing questions; they shouldn't be converted into a cover charge for civic sight.

Commercial legal-data vendors aren't villains merely because they sell better tools. A lawyer may gladly pay for alerts, citators, analytics, collaboration, and polished search (the useful machinery around the record). That value can compete in a market. The underlying filings and orders, however, can't be the captive fuel that keeps the machinery profitable. I mean the raw public material should sit outside the paywall – clean, searchable, downloadable, and available in formats that you can use. Vendors can build above that floor.

Otherwise we get a rigged arcade. The rules are displayed behind glass; the wealthy player buys unlimited turns; everyone else gets a few lives and a blurry view of the scoreboard. Worse, the arcade operator can call this equality because every player faces the same price. That's bullshit. A uniform charge isn't equal access when money determines who can search broadly, catch a change, compare cases, or discover that a supposedly isolated ruling forms a pattern. The game is public power, and our stakes are real.

Digital access changes who can watch institutions without asking permission. When you can inspect the record, you don't have to take a government press release, a corporate statement, or a summary as the final word. You can test the description against the document (and notice what was omitted). I don't claim that every person will become a legal researcher. Most won't. The point is that any person can look, and journalists, librarians, researchers, organizers, litigants, and neighbors can help one another – no blessing required.

A public system doesn't need to mimic every premium database. It needs dependable search, stable links, bulk access where privacy rules allow it, accessible documents, and fees reduced to zero for retrieval. Of course, privacy and safety limits still matter. Sealed material should stay sealed; personal identifiers may require careful handling. Openness isn't a demand to dump every datum into the street. It's a demand that public access work for you in practice – rather than merely exist as a sentence in a rulebook.

I won't pretend that moving the tollbooth solves every inequality in law. It does something smaller and essential: it lets the public see what public power has done. Courts should publish their records through systems anyone can reach, reuse, and understand, while private firms remain free to sell additional services. We can build that road together (and keep the fancy express lanes, if buyers want them). But the road itself is ours. Take down this tollbooth now.
